related_questions.question: Can I get help paying my rent in Massachusetts?

text_blocks.snippet: In Massachusetts, several rental assistance programs are available to help low-income individuals and families pay rent and avoid eviction. These programs include RAFT (Residential Assistance for Families in Transition), ERAP (Emergency Rental Assistance Program), and Section 8 Housing Choice Vouchers. RAFT provides up to $7,000 per 12-month period for rent, utilities, and moving costs. ERAP can offer assistance for rent and utilities accrued during the pandemic. Section 8, also known as the Housing Choice Voucher Program, provides long-term rental assistance.
snippet_highlighted_words: RAFT (Residential Assistance for Families in Transition), ERAP (Emergency Rental Assistance Program), and Section 8 Housing Choice Vouchers

list.title: RAFT (Residential Assistance for Families in Transition):
list.snippet: This program provides emergency rental assistance to help families avoid homelessness or housing instability. It can cover rent arrears, utilities, moving costs, and mortgage payments. RAFT can be used for both current housing and to help families move to new housing.

list.title: ERAP (Emergency Rental Assistance Program):
list.snippet: This program offers financial assistance to renters facing financial hardship due to the pandemic. It can help pay for rent and utility arrears accrued after March 13, 2020, as well as prospective rental assistance.

list.title: Section 8 Housing Choice Voucher Program (HCVP):
list.snippet: This is a federal program that provides long-term rental assistance to low-income families. Vouchers can be used in the private market for a variety of housing options. The amount of assistance is based on income and family size.

list.title: Massachusetts Rental Voucher Program (MRVP):
list.snippet: A state-funded program that provides rental assistance in the form of vouchers, similar to Section 8. Vouchers can be tenant-based (mobile) or project-based.

list.title: Other Programs:
list.snippet: ABCD Action for Boston Community Development and RCAP Solutions offer rental assistance and support to residents in specific areas. Community Action Agencies also offer various housing-related supports.
RAFT: Apply online through Mass.gov or by contacting a regional agency or Housing Consumer Education Center.
ERAP: Call 2-1-1 or visit Mass.gov.
Section 8: Apply through the local housing authority.
MRVP: Apply through the local housing authority.
ABCD: Contact ABCD directly for assistance.
RCAP Solutions: Contact RCAP Solutions directly.
Community Action Agencies: Find your local agency on MASSCAP's website.

related_questions.question: How to apply for cash benefits in mass?

text_blocks.snippet: To apply for cash assistance in Massachusetts, you can apply online through DTA Connect (dtaconnect.com) or by contacting your local Department of Transitional Assistance (DTA) office. DTA Connect is a mobile application and website where you can manage your case and access information. The main cash assistance program is Transitional Aid to Families with Dependent Children (TAFDC).
snippet_highlighted_words: apply online through DTA Connect (dtaconnect.com) or by contacting your local Department of Transitional Assistance (DTA) office

list.title: 1. Online Application:
list.snippet: Go to DTAConnect.com and begin your application for TAFDC.

list.title: 2. Local Office:
list.snippet: If you prefer, you can find your local DTA office and apply in person or by phone.

list.title: 3. Eligibility:
list.snippet: Be prepared to provide information about your household income, assets, and other relevant details to determine eligibility.

list.title: 4. Interview:
list.snippet: You will likely need to participate in an interview to discuss your application.
You can also apply for SNAP (Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program, formerly known as food stamps) through DTA Connect as well.
DTA Connect allows you to manage your case, check your benefits, and get information about other resources.
If you have questions or need help, you can contact 211 or use the EOHLC Resource Locator to find local resources.

related_questions.question: How to apply for mass housing assistance?

text_blocks.snippet: To apply for Massachusetts state-aided public housing, you'll typically use the CHAMP (Common Housing Application for Massachusetts Programs) website. This online portal allows you to apply for various programs based on your desired location. You may also find CHAMP application forms on the Newton Housing Authority website.
snippet_highlighted_words: CHAMP (Common Housing Application for Massachusetts Programs) website

list.title: CHAMP Application:
list.snippet: The primary way to apply for most Massachusetts public housing programs is through the CHAMP website.

list.title: Program Selection:
list.snippet: When applying through CHAMP, you'll select the specific programs you're interested in based on the location where you wish to live.

list.title: Eligibility:
list.snippet: Requirements vary by program, but generally, you'll need to be a Massachusetts resident and meet specific income guidelines. For instance, eligibility for Emergency Assistance (EA) family shelter may include being pregnant or having a child under 21, and having a gross income at or below 115% of the Federal Poverty Guidelines, according to Mass.gov.

list.title: Section 8 Housing Choice Voucher Program:
list.snippet: For federal Section 8 Housing Choice Vouchers, eligibility is generally tied to 50% of the Area Median Income (AMI), according to Mass.gov. Boston's 50% AMI is used to maximize program eligibility for the entire state.

list.title: Waiting Times:
list.snippet: The time it takes to be approved for housing assistance can vary significantly, from a few weeks to several years, depending on factors like bedroom size, preference points, and the availability of units, says the Malden Housing Authority.

list.title: Restrictions:
list.snippet: Certain factors can lead to denial of housing assistance, such as evictions from public housing for drug-related reasons within the past three years, being on a sex offender registry, or convictions for manufacturing methamphetamine on public housing property, according to HUD User (.gov).
